chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Refuge and Bodhichitta I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. (3x) Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. (3x) Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, may everyone be free from misery, may no one ever be separated from their happiness, may everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Seven-Limb Prayer In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time, and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases, and turn the wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Mandala Offering The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, the great mountain, four lands, sun, and moon, seen as a Buddha land and offered thus, may all beings enjoy such pure lands. I offer without any sense of loss the objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion — my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments. Please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Lamrim Prayer The path begins with strong reliance on my kind Teacher, source of all good. O bless me with this understanding, to follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, extremely rare with so much meaning. O bless me with this understanding, all day and night to seize its essence. My body like a water bubble, decays and dies so very quickly. After death come results of karma, just like the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance, bless me to be extremely cautious, always avoiding harmful actions and gathering abundant virtue. Samsara's pleasures are deceptive, give no contentment, only torment. So please bless me to strive sincerely to gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O bless me so that from this pure thought come mindfulness and greatest caution, to keep as my essential practice the doctrine's root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers are drowning in samsara's ocean. O so that I may soon release them, bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha by this alone without three ethics; so bless me with the strength to practice the Bodhisattva's ordination. By pacifying my distractions and analyzing perfect meanings, bless me to quickly gain the union of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container through common paths, bless me to enter the essence practice of good fortune, the supreme vehicle, Vajrayana. The two attainments both depend on my sacred vows and my commitments; bless me to understand this clearly and keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, the way explained by holy Teachers, O bless me to gain both the stages, which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path, and my companions all have long lives; bless me to pacify completely all obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers, and take delight in holy Dharma, accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, and gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings and Purifying From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
The purpose of this meditation is to vastly increase our merit, because we are rejoicing in such meritorious and positive spiritual experiences. In addition to rejoicing in the five Mahayana paths, we will grow our own admiring and wishing faith to attain these states ourselves. The object of meditation is an experience of rejoicing — either really delighting in, or wishing for ourselves, these attainments of the five Mahayana paths. If we reach this experience of rejoicing, we can hold it single-pointedly, deep in our heart.

We can remember that the five paths are: the path of accumulation, preparation, seeing, meditation, and no more learning. When the Bodhisattva attains the path of accumulation, they've developed spontaneous bodhichitta, tranquil abiding on the mind of bodhichitta, and will never become an ordinary samsaric being again. They will never turn back ever again. In addition, within the path of accumulation, we attain the realization of the Dharma continuum, where we can remember our past lives and all the Dharma teachings that we've received, even communicate with Buddhas directly. Just rejoice. How wonderful this will be for us.

From there, we will evolve to the path of preparation, where we will attain superior seeing — tranquil abiding on emptiness with our mind of bodhichitta. Just imagine and delight how wonderful that would be. Every moment of every day, every thought is not separate from our remembering emptiness.

This in turn will evolve into the path of seeing, where we realize emptiness directly, free of a generic image or conceptuality. At this stage, even if our body was cut, it would just seem like space being cut, and we have no more intellectually-formed delusions. At this stage, we're also able to emanate for a hundred beings and engage in many more incredibly powerful spiritual actions. Just really rejoice in this.

This in turn evolves into the path of meditation, where we progress along the ten grounds of a Bodhisattva and gain greater and greater capabilities to benefit others, and attain the surpassing perfections of giving, moral discipline, patience, and so forth. Just rejoice how joyful and incredible that will be, as we progress through these paths and grounds.

Finally, we will enter the path of no more learning and attain enlightenment, fulfilling our own and others' wishes. At this point, our deep peace will radiate eternally as compassion, gradually drawing all beings to the same state. And as we consider all these spiritual attainments, simply imagine what it would be like to reach them. And when a strong feeling of rejoicing arises, just hold that single-pointedly for the remainder of the practice.

And then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

dataShares.speaker: Alexis
dataShares.text:
I was with Ryan last week with the five paths, and I'm glad, wherever he is, that he said that, because I know that the first time, the tenth time, the hundredth time I've heard it, it's overwhelming, especially even the first part. I don't even think I'm up the hill yet. So what helped me was just kind of figuring out, and it was when we did the Lamrim, and there was one that was difficult for me. I wasn't even near that part. And then you said something like, what if a little, or what if there's a chance — that you put into some wording. I should have written it down, and I did not.

And then I looked at the path again, and it was kind of like, well, what if I get closer to accumulation? Like each day, like getting closer, you do something, merit, and be like, okay, I'm closer to accumulation. And it just seemed like a little possible. So I just wanted to share that — just those words that you said, just a little bit closer, or more so, or something like that. It just feels nice.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks, Alexis. It's a good point. It's about being incremental and gradual. In Buddhist practice, we're talking about very high-minded things, and we do need to talk about them. You can't just live in the kiddie pool forever, in the shallow end, because it's safe. We can't just live there forever. It's actually not safe.

So we do need to talk about bigger things. And to not do it is an utter disservice. That's not the purpose of this meditation center — it's to lead people to Buddhahood. So we can't just talk about the least common denominator, the thing that we can all fully accept and already agree with. If we just stay there, none of us will ever grow — just be an echo chamber of ordinariness. It's very disappointing, and there's enough places to do that. So we have to think big. We have to imagine. Bigger, bigger, bigger, bigger. We have to keep expanding our mind.

So on one hand, we have to do that over and over and over again. The nice thing about the Lamrim is you're doing that repeatedly. Enlightenment! Freedom from samsara! Realizing emptiness! Enlightenment again! Bodhichitta! Great compassion for all living beings, including all of your mortal enemies! It just keeps pushing the mind out of this ordinary, tiny place.

But as you noted, at some point that can feel also a little bit overwhelming, or a little bit distant, or just abstract. So we have to always balance our practice with, okay, I do need big picture, always. I need the big picture. But I also need to know where I'm at, and how to incrementally move in that direction. Those are kind of two functions in our mind. Big picture gives us a whole map and a direction. We need that, or else we're going to incrementally go nowhere. But if we just think big picture and we don't approach our practice in some incremental way, asking, what's the next step for me? What's the next thing that can move me forward? Then we're just going to be thinking big picture but not going to move forward at all. So we do need a balance of those two skills.

So yeah, that was the point. I think it was about bodhichitta or something like that. You're asking, becoming enlightened feels a little far away. And then it was like, okay, that's fine. We still need to keep thinking about it. But then today, what about just aiming to get a little bit more enlightened? We can all do that. It's a great point. It's a good teaching skill, too — if we're teaching a Dharma class, we don't want to shy away from big picture. But we also need to make sure we pepper in some good incremental stuff. Thank you.

dataShares.speaker: Anne K
dataShares.text:
I just want to talk a little bit about yesterday. I really loved when you said if we do the six sessions and our Vajrayogini mantra commitment, we've got a perfect tantric practice. I've never thought about it like that before.

And when I was chatting about it with my discussion partner, we were talking about how when you're not fulfilling your commitment, even if you're not conscious of it, you're disturbed. And how beautiful it would be to know that I was fulfilling my commitment and that I can do it so easily. And I thought about it this morning and it felt like such a relief.

And I was sharing earlier that I'm like, part of this is like, I can do more. And I'm like, no, don't try to. Just commit to doing what you're supposed to do. Just do that for a while. Get it down so it becomes like second nature. And knowing — it makes me want to cry, the simplicity of it — and knowing that I can fulfill my commitment easily. It really is easy. I can do it no matter what. So I'm feeling very inspired by that today.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks, Anne. Thanks for sharing that. It's just so important. That little feeling like I'm not doing enough is an incredibly nasty little Mara. And the problem with that Mara is that it doesn't care about how much we're doing. It's an insatiable Mara that will scale with you forever. So it's a Mara. It's not based on rationality or sensibility. It's not based on kindness or wisdom. It's just there to destroy our practice.

So expanding our practice never comes from 'I'm not doing enough.' It comes from 'I want to benefit people more. I'm excited about increasing my capacity to benefit people more.' That's very different than 'I'm not doing enough.' Those are very different minds.

It's like a friend of mine is this amazing doctor. She's a Dharma practitioner and doctor. And she at some point went back for some real continuing ed because there was something she was really passionate about. And it was just like, I want to help people more. And she was so busy already, mind-bogglingly busy. A parent, in the ER all day. And she took on a ton more. But it was like play for her. She felt like she was winning by adding it. It's what she wanted because she wanted to help more and she saw the pathway to do that.

So we have to be careful about this little Mara. We don't want to let that Mara even be an advisor on the council of our mind. We don't want to let them sit at the table. They don't get a vote. They don't get to weigh in. And if they speak up, we just say, shut up. Like that. Shut up. You're not me. You're a Mara. Shut up. We're not saying it to ourselves. We're saying it to the Mara. Go away. Bye.

If we actually just know what the commitment is, then we realize it's actually incredibly easy. It's very easy. And then if we can't do that commitment, then we find something that we can do. And there's no one going to police us. It's us and our guru who can talk about it.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.text:
I really appreciate this idea of expanding the boundary of what we think is possible for ourselves and trying to really live at that frontier. And yesterday's workshop was really helpful for that. I feel like my tantric practice kind of sits really nicely in there. And whenever I do it, I always think about emptiness. And just doing it reminds me to think about emptiness more and more.

At the same time, I have a sort of confession, which is that my mind has a tendency also — there's no guarantee that we keep moving in the right direction. So there was this pivotal moment. We moved, my wife and I moved just around the block a few weeks ago. And as we were packing up our stuff, there was this old video game system. I was like, I think we should get rid of this. And my wife — I'm not blaming her at all, but this is what happened — she said, no, we should keep it. It could actually be a benefit. If your nephews or nieces come around, we could play with them. I said, okay, good idea.

And then as we were setting up the new apartment, I was like, you know what a perfect place for that video game system would be? And then all of a sudden, after not playing for years, I now re-picked up this habit that does nothing to benefit others or grow my own abilities. And all of a sudden, I was making time to do this thing.

It was actually just this morning. After yesterday's workshop, I was like, okay, I have to pack up this thing. And I put it away. It was like, I don't know, when your mom throws away your baseball cards or something. This kind of moment. So hopefully I stick to it.

Another thing you mentioned yesterday was about how we prioritize things. Sort of taking all the things we do and laying them out on the table and working a little bit from first principles about what's the most important thing, what's the second most important thing. If you're actually spending your precious time in this life doing something, then hopefully it's because it's important. And just doing that analysis helped me to see it more clearly. Anyway, I hope to spend more time at that frontier and less time going back to what I've always been doing.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks, David. Nice explanation of what's going on. I think it all makes sense. Just knowing — it's just like a little classic Mara trick. It's always like, just a little. That little voice. Just a little.

It's like you're at a store and there's people selling perfume or something. And they're like, oh, just a free sample. Just put a little on your wrist. Give it a little sniff. They are greedy people. They're not giving away perfume for free. They want money. And they know giving it away for free is the best way to make money. Why is that? Because 'just a little' tricks our mind. It tricks our barriers and boundaries and our moral discipline. Somehow in our mind we go, oh, that's different than breaking that rule I have for myself. A little somehow isn't breaking the rule. And then ten years later we drag ourselves out of the hole that came from just a little.

We just all have to know what is our version of that. I have that with things like video games, computer games. I have a zero rule for that. I bet if I played that game for one minute, you guys would never see me again. Just gone. For some reason that triggers my karma into an insane, feral, crazy state. I have to know myself and know my karma. That's a zero thing for me. For some people they hate video games but shopping is their version. Or gardening.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.text:
I've made a commitment to do something that in the beginning I didn't really want to do. You know what it is. I don't feel competent or confident in it and it's been very overwhelming. You can hear my voice. When we sat down to meditate today, as soon as we started the prayer, I felt like I was going to cry. Which made me grateful to be here because this is —

My practice this week has been recognizing this anxiety and throwing bodhichitta at it. That I took this on because it's going to help a lot of people. Besides helping me, it's going to help me help more people, not just in fulfilling this commitment but in my future within the Dharma community.

But it's very hard. I've just been struggling with having those feelings fit into the rest of my life and being able to do other commitments. Because I feel like I have to be working on this, but I don't want to. But I'm not going to work on that other thing that I have to work on either, because I should be doing this. I'm just going to go play a word puzzle or clean out the basement or whatever it is.

It's not really a negative. It's just not something that I really was — ooh, I want to talk about it. But the throwing bodhichitta at it has been helpful.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.note: Increasing capacity through lojong and courage
dataShares.text:
Thanks, Fran. It's definitely not negative. It's an important and really helpful thing to share. There's a practice as we increase our bodhichitta of increasing our capacity. It has to do with our lojong practice of understanding that suffering has many good qualities and that overcoming self-cherishing and self-grasping is also painful. It's not fun until it's basically over.

For many people, when the pain comes, they retract. The pain threshold is where they retract. Whether it's anxiety pain or physical pain or pressure or whatever. So it's like, go, go, go — oh, there's the pain — retract.

In the practice of lojong, though, it's designed to help us cross that threshold, because it's not really there. Pain isn't there from its own side. The mind is imputing pain, whatever it is, physical, mental, whatever. So in the lojong practices, we have many different techniques, because we want to benefit others and become enlightened, we learn how to transmute pain and face pain and go against it and be okay even being in pain, so that one day we can become completely free. So it's really a path of courage.

In these kind of cases, when we're doing something because we want to grow our capacity and to benefit others more, we are knowingly going into battle, knowing the pain is going to come. The thing is, that's not negative at all. That's incredibly brave. That's courageous. It's not fun usually. It's not fun to go into battle and experience the pain of those minds coming up. But that's the way through — to learn how to not be afraid of that pain and learn how to traverse that gap, or even transgress against that wall that the delusions make.

So to me it's like an example of bravery. It doesn't mean it's fun. But it does make us grow our capacity for the benefit of others instead of retract. And then that capacity in the long run will make us very powerful and very capable. Thank you. Thanks for sharing. I think it's great.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB reading: Dedicating Merit (pp. 121-122, ¶456-465). Why anger destroys merit.
teaching.text:
Dedication. Dedication is a prayer made at the conclusion of a specific practice so that the positive energy of the practice will be directed toward a specific result. This committing positive energy or merit is like a horse that will carry us in whichever direction we determine by means of our dedication. If the merit of a virtuous action is dedicated to the attainment of birth as a human or god, that action will become the cause for rebirth in those realms. Similarly, if we dedicate for the attainment of liberation, enlightenment, development of bodhichitta, for the realization of emptiness, the merit will ripen as directed.

In this chapter, the merit generated from the first six limbs of practice is dedicated for the sake of all sentient beings. When we practice in the Mahayana tradition, we should always remember to dedicate our accumulated merit for the generation of the precious mind of bodhichitta. This is the purpose of the prayer: may the precious bodhichitta grow where it has not yet grown, and where it has grown may it not decrease but flourish forevermore. This is a verse from Shantideva.

There are important things to remember at the end of any virtuous action. If we want that action to be pure and effective, we should make sure that our initial motivation is uncontaminated and correct. Then, when the action is completed, we should dedicate the merit generated towards the desired goal. Without a pure motivation, our meditation will not be a pure Dharma practice, and without proper dedication, the aim of our meditation will not be fulfilled.

So again, if you don't understand that, think dependent relationship. Dependently related flowers, a dependently related offering to a dependently related Buddha. Empty flowers, empty offering, empty Buddha.

If the merit of our virtuous actions is not dedicated, many hindrances can arise. Merit left undedicated is like a door left unlocked, and anger is the thief capable of stealing whatever merit we may have created. However, if the merit of a virtuous action has been properly dedicated towards bodhichitta, no amount of future anger will be able to destroy it. Thus, it is very important that we conclude all our actions with a complete and heartfelt dedication.

Why is anger so destructive for our merit? Why is it anger that destroys all our merit?

teaching.speaker: Alexis
teaching.text: Isn't it the strong — I think in the last class we were talking about anger and how it's like the strongest delusion, the worst delusion you can have.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, it is. It's probably the most sort of powerfully violent delusion, yeah. But why would that be the case?

teaching.speaker: Byron
teaching.text: It's the very opposite of renunciation. It's completely — it's the end result of self-grasping, self-cherishing to its nth degree. It's like going the exact opposite direction from the way we're supposed to be going.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Why anger destroys merit; dedicating with imagination
teaching.text:
Yeah, that's basically it. Because if we think, what's merit? Merit is the cause to attain a Buddha's form body. And why does one try to get a body of a Buddha? It's to benefit all living beings. And anger — it's harming living beings. It wants to harm living beings. It's not only relating to them as inherently existent. It's relating to them and us as inherently existent. The situation is inherently existent. Then it's relating to us as superior to that person. And then relating to them as so low that we not only don't care about them — which is just apathy, normal self-cherishing — we actually want to harm them.

So each layer is another compound of delusion. Once we've gotten to anger, it's like six levels of delusion built on each other in the opposite direction of where our merit is designed to go. Attachment has some levels of delusion — ignorance, self-cherishing, wishing to find happiness outside ourselves. But anger has more on top of that. It usually involves wanting to harm other people. You can just be attached and eat Cheetos all day — that's not harming anyone particularly. But anger is, I want to harm you. It's gone way farther than the attached mind.

teaching.speaker: Anne K
teaching.text: I don't understand why the anger actually destroys the merit. I can see why it would produce negative karma — add like ten points of negative karma to your existing karma bundle. But why would it actually destroy the merit? That's what I've never been able to figure out.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, good thing to think about. Fran, yeah.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: I don't have an answer for that. I was thinking how anger is the one delusion that's aimed at other people. My anxiety is aimed at me. I mean, I can be angry at myself as well. But real anger is, as you said, the intent to harm. But it's almost primarily aimed at other living beings.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, exactly. And then there are a few other ones — miserliness, malice, covetousness, resentment. But anger is a stand-in for all the anger-related ones. Part of the thing about how anger destroys our merit is — one of the ways to ponder it is that they're dependently related. Dependently related merit. Dependently related anger. How are they intermingling? Because they're not in siloed areas. Our merit or karma is not broken off from everything else. It's all an interdependent web. So that would be the key to figuring out how anger destroys it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Dedicating with imagination; Ch. 10 of Guide
teaching.text:
The other thing I'll say on dedication is, when we dedicate, we should imagine the results that we're dedicating for. It's not a prayer into the void. We're imagining and creating the results in our mind. And if you need help with that, you can go through chapter 10 of Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life, which is the dedication chapter, where Shantideva gives us incredible, flowing dedication.

Traditionally, Buddhists, when they do some really virtuous action, would do chapter 10 dedication as a way to dedicate really extensively. And you'll see there's incredible imagery. For example, you imagine appearing in the hell realms and pouring rain down on all the hell beings and cooling their heat and appearing with them and shooing away the Maras. So we can bring in extensive imagination into our dedication practice. That's the point.
